title: Long-End Rates Are High Not Because Policy Is Weak, but Because AI Data Centers Are Competing for Funds
dek: Kansas City Fed President Schmid said at Jackson Hole that the 30-year Treasury yield above 5% is the result of AI and data centers competing for funds; his personal view is that monetary conditions remain relatively loose, and inflation running in the mid-3s must be addressed.
why: Fed officials rarely explain long-end rates, AI physical crowding out, and the dissent mechanism so directly; however, the task force and the new chair's roadmap remain vague, so don't expect this episode to provide answers.
who: Macro traders focused on the Fed's path, rates strategists, and policy researchers studying how AI infrastructure transmits to inflation and the real economy.
skip: The first minute of pleasantries and the last minute of social media information can be skipped.

points.h: The Endpoint of Payments Innovation Is Making Payments Boring
points.body: Schmid said the Fed's goal is to make payments boring: settling $5 to $10 trillion daily through multiple pipelines, and future technology will eliminate frictions like float and fees, achieving atomic settlement—funds transfer and reconciliation instantaneously. On one hand, this is highly innovative; on the other, it will bring disruptive shocks, so it's necessary to discuss how to maintain certainty on an instant system. This sets the stage for the conference theme: payments innovation is not a technology problem but a settlement and liquidity problem.

points.h: An Instant Settlement World Requires Repricing Liquidity
points.body: Asked about the link between bond yields and the conference theme, Schmid brought the discussion back to two words: duration and liquidity. If payments are instant, there must be verified liquidity behind them to complete settlement. With positive economic growth and inflation not yet back to 2%, the yield curve will reprice at a more normal level. In other words, high long-end rates are not just a result of monetary policy but the entire system repricing the liquidity and duration required by an instant settlement world.

points.h: Baby Boomer Retirement Drains Experience, Not Just Manpower
points.body: Schmid said his baby boomer generation is retiring at about 4 million people per year, and in the past three months he has signed more retirement letters than in the previous three years. This creates both opportunities and risks: he worries about losing 'intellectual muscle,' so he repeatedly asks his Fed economists and bankers: how to use AI to translate the experience of 65-year-old retirees to those who are now 25, 35, or 45, rather than waiting until they are 55 or 65 to learn. Immigration policy also has an impact, but this process will last a decade and ultimately be net positive for the economy.

points.h: The AI Boom Is Pushing Up Prices of Steel and Copper
points.body: Asked whether businesses in his district feel the 'real crowding out effect' of data centers, Schmid answered 'I hear it every day.' Demand from data centers for machinery, steel, copper, and other commodities directly transmits to other industries, and even agricultural futures have risen. His approach is to use an onion-peeling decomposition to judge what percentage of current growth comes from the boom effect of AI/data centers. This is crucial for his judgment on 'whether inflation can be pushed back to 2%'—not looking at GDP broadly, but breaking it down to see which sectors are overheating.

points.h: Employment Is Fine, but Inflation Doesn't Allow a Pivot Now
points.body: Schmid publicly acknowledged: the labor market is in a good place, but the inflation task is not complete. The closer you get to 2%, the harder the decisions become—everyone fears overshooting, and the potential error is being too slow or too aggressive. Recent inflation running in the mid-3s must be addressed. He called his recent dissents 'considered dissents' and believes this is exactly the debate atmosphere Warsh wants: the Fed has an obligation to manage inflation to 2% and should have the ability to do so.

points.h: Dissenting Is Not Emotion but Different Risk Weighting
points.body: Schmid explained his decision threshold for past dissents: the FOMC has 19 people, each with their own team; his role is as a 'communication transmitter,' bringing the concerns of business owners and local leaders from the seven states of the Tenth District to the table, and then bringing FOMC discussions back to the district. Dissent is not emotion but a mechanism—expressing 'I think the risk weighting between the two goals of maximum employment and inflation is different from what you estimate.' He believes this is the most valuable part of FOMC discussions.

points.h: The Neutral Rate Floor Is Higher; Current Policy Is Actually Loose
points.body: Schmid said that if he had the 2008 cycle and the pandemic cycle in front of him, he wouldn't second-guess the policies of that time; the more accurate framework now is that 'r-star is normalizing,' but its underlying level may be higher than before 2008. Therefore, his personal judgment is that current interest rates are in a relatively loose position, and the Fed needs to continue discussions around the relative position of r-star and the yield curve. This statement directly supports his stance that 'inflation is not complete and monetary policy should not ease prematurely.'

points.h: The Fed Shouldn't Make the Front Page; Markets Must Price Risk Themselves
points.body: Schmid quoted Warsh's view: the Fed would rather be on page B12 than the front page—meaning the central bank should not aspire to headline news but should stay low-key while ensuring the payment system and technology run robustly. His expectation for the task force is to re-examine data sets and communication methods, clarifying which communications are effective and which are not; more importantly, the market itself must take on the function of pricing risk, and the Fed's communication cannot make the market fragile. He also revealed: so far, there has been no substantive dialogue between the task force and the regional Fed presidents.

terms.def: A settlement method where fund transfer and reconciliation occur simultaneously and instantly, eliminating frictions like float and fees.
The neutral interest rate: the real rate that neither stimulates nor restrains economic growth, serving as a reference for judging monetary policy tightness.
The rule by which a central bank adjusts policy in response to economic data and fiscal/legislative outcomes.
A communication tool where the central bank pre-announces its future policy path; Warsh explicitly dislikes it.
The Fed's two statutory goals assigned by Congress: stable prices and maximum employment.
A vote against the majority decision by an FOMC member, expressing a different judgment on the risk weighting between the two goals.
